# {#introduction}

::: {.centered}
<img src="images/cloud-bleeding.png" style="max-height: 90%; max-width: 90%; margin-top: -50px;" />
:::

::: {.notes}
Our main goal is to stop cloud waste, and while there are many ways to do this,
some even works, such as:

- identifying idle resources
- automatically scaling down resources when they're not needed
- deleting unused resources or migrating e.g. to cheaper storage tiers etc

We focus on:
:::

# {#no-cloud transition="convex-in slide-out" .center}

::: {.centered}
  <img src="images/no-cloud-just-another-comp.png" style="max-width: 75%; max-height: 50%;" />
:::

::: {.notes}
While pretty much everyone understands that cloud is still just another computer,
at a remote location, that I can spin up quickly and throw away as needed,
BUT we often don't really know what kind of computer that is.
:::

## {#old-vs-new transition="slide-in fade-out"}

::: {.notes}
Before the cloud, you could simply walk to the server, and
it was not too difficult to say that the computer running your program

- is a potato
- or a commodity PC with a case that has started turning yellow over the years
- or it's a bleeding edge, high-end server
- or not so new and it still has a turbo button

You could even open up the case when the system administrator was not watching ...

BUT nowadays
:::

::: {.centered}
<div style="position: relative; display: inline-block; margin-top: -45px;">
  <img src="images/small-big-computer.jpg" style="display: block; width: 100%;">
</div>
:::


## {#vcpu transition="fade-in slide-out"}  

::: {.notes}
Like what on earth is even a virtual CPU?! Right?

There's a conceptual uncertainty and massive visibility problem here,
as a vCPU could range from an overprovisioned, poor-performing thread with saturated bandwidth to memory,
versus a dedicated CPU core of a state-of-the-art server -- with massive CPU cache and high memory bandwidth.

Which means that your applications could run much much faster!
:::

::: {.centered}

::: {.notes}

Any ideas how much faster is the best performing vCPU compared to the slowest?
I don't mean a comparing cloud servers with hundreds of cores with a potato,
indeed just focusing on the single-core performance -- like doing as many integer divisions in a second as possible.
:::

## {#vcpu-benchmarking transition="slide-in slide-out"}

::: {.notes}
Well, we measured! Not only these 2 servers, but actually close to 4,000 (3,800)!

So we solve this visibility problem of the cloud by burning hundreds of thousands of dollars to
start servers, measure performance, and calculate cost-efficiency,
then publish these results and related tooling with open licenses,
so that you can save money by optimizing your cloud spend.

DATA DRIVEN way

<script>
  (function () {
    function initVcpuCountSlide() {
      var reveal = window.Reveal;
      var slide = document.getElementById('vcpus-2-count');
      if (!reveal || !slide) return false;
      if (slide.dataset.vcpuCountBound) return true;

      slide.dataset.vcpuCountBound = '1';

      function getChartSvg() {
        var obj = slide.querySelector('object.vcpu-count-chart');
        if (!obj || !obj.contentDocument) return null;
        return obj.contentDocument.getElementById('vcpu-count-chart');
      }

      function syncZoom() {
        var chart = getChartSvg();
        var fragment = slide.querySelector('.vcpu-count-zoom');
        if (!chart || !fragment) return;
        chart.classList.toggle('zoomed', fragment.classList.contains('visible'));
      }

      var obj = slide.querySelector('object.vcpu-count-chart');
      if (obj) {
        obj.addEventListener('load', syncZoom);
        if (obj.contentDocument) syncZoom();
      }

      reveal.on('fragmentshown', function (event) {
        if (event.fragment && event.fragment.classList.contains('vcpu-count-zoom')) syncZoom();
      });
      reveal.on('fragmenthidden', function (event) {
        if (event.fragment && event.fragment.classList.contains('vcpu-count-zoom')) syncZoom();
      });
      reveal.on('slidechanged', function (event) {
        if (event.currentSlide && event.currentSlide.id === 'vcpus-2-count') syncZoom();
      });

      window.addEventListener('message', function (event) {
        if (event.data && event.data.type !== 'vcpu-count-click') return;
        if (!slide.classList.contains('present')) return;
        var fragment = slide.querySelector('.vcpu-count-zoom');
        if (fragment && !fragment.classList.contains('visible')) reveal.nextFragment();
      });

      return true;
    }

    if (!initVcpuCountSlide()) {
      var tries = 0;
      var timer = setInterval(function () {
        if (initVcpuCountSlide() || ++tries > 50) clearInterval(timer);
      }, 100);
    }
  })();
</script>

# $ apropos sparecores.com {#apropos transition="convex-in convex-out"}

<ul style="font-size: 0.9em;">
  <li class="fragment">Open-source tools, database schemas and documentation to inspect and inventory cloud vendors and their offerings, including pricing and measured performance.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Managed infrastructure, databases, APIs, SDKs, and web applications to make this data publicly accessible.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Open-source helpers to select, start and manage instances in your own environment.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Open-source Python/R packages and workflow orchestration extensions (e.g. Metaflow) to track resource usage and cost of DS/ML/AI jobs. Open-source tooling to right-size instances.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Add-on services to scale data science workflows, even without direct vendor engagement.</li>
</ul>

::: {.notes}
- so Spare Cores is an open-source ecosystem, including software, database schemas, guides,
- and actual databases if you don't want to run the ETL tooling yourself .. also providing APIs, SDKs etc to make it easier to query data
- unified CLI to start machines
- and working on an an optional SaaS offering built on the top of the open-source tooling for folks who would rather avoid registering with all cloud providers etc: give us a Docker image, a command to run, and you credit card .. all set, we will run it wherever it's cheapest.
:::

# {#gilty}

::: {.centered}
<img style="width:60%; margin-top: -50px;" src="images/gilty-coffee.png" />
:::

::: {.notes}

[[A]] Back to **GILty** — **pure Python** app

- **latency** + **throughput** → **single-core** (and cache) speed must be high
  - more CPUs -> more throughput, but no **help for latency**
- ran **GILty** on a few **AWS** instance types → measured **speed**
- SC DB: which **benchmarks** **correlate** with those results?
  - proxy: **PassMark CPU Single Threaded** — rank machines without re-running GILty everywhere
:::

## {#gilty-and-friends}

::: {.centered}
<img src="images/kcd-budapest-teaser.jpg" style="max-height: 90%; max-width: 90%; margin-top: -50px;" />
:::

::: {.notes}
[[A]] **GIL** history — for folks who **don't know the GIL** yet  
- image: **G(H)uido** v(F)an Rossum + **Larry** Hastings (Gilectomy)  
- **GIL** since early 90s · serializes Python bytecode · **more cores ≠ faster** for pure Python  
- **Greg Stein** 1996 patch · parts landed, GIL stayed  
- **Gilectomy** (**Larry Hastings**, ~2016): real PoC, fine-grained locks — **overhead** killed it (Guido: no single-thread regression)  
- **Sam Gross** nogil → **PEP 703** (2023): optional **free-threaded** build  
- **3.13** experimental · **3.14** officially supported, **not default** · **3.15** Stable ABI `abi3t`  
- for **GILty**-class apps: promising **if** you redesign for threads + deps support · else still need **fast single core**  
- working name for this project: **"Core Alone"** — fits, right?
:::

# $ strace -e environment gilty.py

**Before:** **AWS** · **EKS** · **Cluster Autoscaler** + **fixed node groups**  
→ capacity, not **single-core** / **latency**

Then: **Karpenter** → **EKS Auto mode**  
→ dynamic EC2 pick under load — easy

But Karpenter AWS filters: family · cpu count · gen · …  
plus `instance-cpu-sustained-clock-speed-mhz` — **vendor clock**, not a **benchmark**  
→ **how do we pick the fastest core for GILty?**

::: {.notes}
[[A]] path to the gap

- **before:** CAS + fixed node groups — bad fit for **GILty**  
- moved to **Karpenter**, then **EKS Auto mode** — flexible instance lists  
- closest to “speed”: `karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-cpu-sustained-clock-speed-mhz` (EC2 `SustainedClockSpeedInGhz` → MHz)  
- that’s **catalog GHz**, not measured single-thread · cache/IPC matter · GILty ≠ GHz ranking  
- still missing: **PassMark / Geekbench**-style pick
:::

## PassMark ST vs catalog GHz {#passmark-vs-ghz}

::: {.centered}
<img src="images/aws-passmark-vs-ghz.png" style="width: 92%; margin-top: -30px;" />
:::

::: {.notes}
[[A]] glance at the chart

- ~**a thousand** AWS types · GHz vs PassMark single-thread  
- trends up, but look at the **vertical stacks** — same clock, very different scores  
- so Karpenter’s MHz filter ≠ **fastest core** for **GILty**
:::

## Same GHz, how wide is PassMark? {#passmark-ghz-spread}

::: {.centered}
<img src="images/aws-passmark-ghz-spread.png" style="max-height: 520px; width: auto; margin-top: -40px;" />
:::

<p style="font-size: 0.85em; text-align: center; margin-top: 0;">
Within one clock band: up to about **+200%** PassMark ST spread
</p>

::: {.notes}
[[A]] same GHz → max PassMark gap

- each bar = one catalog GHz · **(max − min) / min**  
- some bands **double+** (~**+100%**…**+200%**)  
- red ≈ bad · GHz alone won’t pick the **fast core**
:::

## Just set the filter to 5 GHz? {#just-5ghz}

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
Simple idea: `instance-cpu-sustained-clock-speed-mhz >= 5000`

| | **r5a.large** | **c8a.large** | **m8azn.large** (5 GHz) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| PassMark ST | ~1400 | ~3800 | ~4300 |
| on-demand | ~\$0.11 | ~\$0.11 | ~\$0.21 |
| regions | ~16 | ~7 | **~6** |

- only **~16** types · **2** families · ~**1%** of AWS catalog  
- **~2×** the money for ~**+10%** PassMark vs **c8a**  
- tiny fallback pool → **capacity / spot** pain
:::

::: {.notes}
[[A]] “then just require 5 GHz?”

- **tiny menu** — handful of SKUs, mostly **m8azn** / **x8aedz**  
- **few regions** · new / niche  
- **m8azn.large** ≈ **twice** **c8a.large** price · only a bit faster  
- **x8aedz** = huge RAM tax  
- Karpenter wants **diversity** — 5 GHz pin = brittle  
- need **benchmark ranking**, not a GHz floor
:::

# $ claude --plan "fix problem"

::: {style="font-size: 0.72em;"}
Pub talk → need **benchmark**-ranked types in **Karpenter** (incl. **EKS Auto**)

**Plan** (`sc-karpenter-nodepool` ADRs + sequenced v1 plans):

1. **Own NodePools only** — never patch user pools / no `NodeOverlay`  
   → **managed** Karpenter **+ GitOps** (Argo CD, …) — no fights over a shared object
2. **`SCNodePool` → one NodePool** — template verbatim + selected `instance-type` list
3. Emit **universal keys only** (`instance-type` · arch · capacity)  
   → avoid **RequirementsDrifted** loops
4. **Selectors + ranking** from **Keeper** (e.g. PassMark ST · family band)
5. **Churn control** — 24h refresh · hysteresis · never empty list
6. **Go / kubebuilder** — reuse Karpenter validation + provider test fakes
:::

::: {.notes}
[[A]] how we designed it (with Claude)

- problem: Karpenter has **shape + price**, not **measured single-core**  
- constraint: **EKS Auto Mode** → can't fork Karpenter / patch their pools  
- also: **GitOps** (Argo CD, …) — don't mutate a pool the user owns → sync wars  
- **ADR-001:** create **our own** NodePools only  
- **ADR-003:** one **`SCNodePool`** → one NodePool  
- **ADR-004:** only stamp keys every provider accepts — else **drift loop**  
- **ADR-002:** read **Keeper API**, filter/rank client-side  
- **ADR-006:** **churn** — don't replace nodes every time the ranking wiggles  
- **ADR-007:** **Go** so we import Karpenter's own validators  
- plans 01→08: scaffold → selection → adapters → controller → tests → Helm  
- next: **demo** the result
:::

# ENTRYPOINT ["sc-karpenter-nodepool"]

::: {style="font-size: 0.65em;"}
Great for **picking** types · **not** for inspector-style **multi-cloud JIT**

**Limitations** (vs “pod annotation → any cloud / region / AZ / SKU”):

::: {.incremental}
- **not a provisioner** — only writes a Karpenter `NodePool` (`instance-type` list)
- **one cloud · one cluster** — regions from NodeClass / node labels, not per-pod
- **no cross-cloud / cross-region hop** in one request (AWS≠GCP≠Hetzner from one Pod)
- **needs Karpenter + cloud provider** already there (**EKS / Auto · AKS NAP · GKE · …**)
- **no** VPC / image import / Flatcar join / mesh — that's **not** this controller
- Pod **can** pin a type (`node.kubernetes.io/instance-type`) — but only if it's **already in the pool**  
  · no “**any** vendor · **any** region · **this** SKU” from one annotation (≠ `start.yml`)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[[A]] can we run **sc-inspector** on this?

- today **`start.yml`**: GH Actions + Pulumi · pick **vendor + instance** · start VM  
- dream: Pod asks for **exact** type (and cloud/region) → node appears → isolate → tear down  
- **yes**, Pod can use **nodeSelector / affinity** on `instance-type` — Karpenter will prefer/launch that  
  · **if** that type is in the generated **NodePool** (SC selection / ranking)  
- **no**: one Pod cannot jump to **another cloud/region** — pool is still **this** cluster’s provider  
- still need **multi-vendor provider + join** → next slide (**scarpenter** / ROADMAP)
:::

# $ cat sc-karpenter-nodepool/ROADMAP.md

::: {style="font-size: 0.72em;"}
Ideal stack for **sc-inspector** (replace GH Actions + Pulumi `start.yml`):

::: {.incremental}
- **Control plane:** on-prem / cheap VMs — **k3s** (3 servers) · **not** EKS/GKE/AKS
- **Mesh:** **Headscale** tailnet — workers need **outbound only** (any cloud/region)
- **Orchestration:** **Hatchet** — plan runs · create inspector Pods · retries / timeouts
- **Provisioner:** **scarpenter** — multi-vendor **Karpenter** provider + **sc-keeper** catalog
- **Nodes:** **Flatcar** + Ignition · TLS bootstrap join · **single-tenant** · die when empty
- **Flow:** Pod `nodeSelector` (vendor/type) → pending → cheapest offering → boot → inspect → **tear down**

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[[A]] what we’d build for Spare Cores inspector

- today: **`start.yml`** every 15m · Pulumi stacks · idle VMs · git as state  
- want: **Pod-driven JIT** · any of **8 clouds** · join **our** cluster · kill node when done  
- **k3s + Headscale** — CP anywhere · nodes behind NAT OK  
- **Hatchet** replaces the GH schedule / retry spaghetti  
- **scarpenter** = the missing piece (multi-cloud Karpenter) — **not** sc-karpenter-nodepool alone  
- Flatcar everywhere · generic kubelet join · consolidateAfter ≈ **0**  
- sc-karpenter-nodepool stays useful: **which** types · **PassMark** / price band  
- design: `sc-docs/k8s-inspector` · ask the room if they’d use this → next slide
:::
